1.open: When did you last wait a long time for something to be made right, like a refund, a repair, or an apology? How did you handle the wait?
questions: Paul says he is thankful because "your faith is growing more and more, and your love for one another is increasing" (v. 3). Where have you seen faith or love grow in a church or group you have been part of, even in a hard season?
The church was enduring "all the persecution and affliction" (v. 4). What do you think daily life was like for a believer in Thessalonica, and what might it have cost them to keep following Jesus?
Paul says their suffering is "clear evidence of God's righteous judgment" (v. 5). That is a hard thing to hear. How do you think the Thessalonians heard it, and how do you hear it?
Verse 7 promises "relief to you who are oppressed." What does relief look like to you right now, and what part of life do you most wish God would set right?
Verses 6 to 9 speak of God repaying those who cause affliction. Some people find this comforting and others find it troubling. Which is closer to your reaction, and why?

Verse 9 speaks of "eternal destruction." Christians read this in different ways, and your group may too. What questions does this verse raise for you, and what do you feel sure of about God's character?

Paul prays that God "will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith" (v. 11). What good desire do you have that feels too small or too weak to matter? What would it mean to ask God for power to carry it out?
Verse 12 says all of this happens "according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ." How does grace change the way you read a chapter about endurance and judgment?
1.life: Think of one person you know who is going through something hard. This week, write or say a simple word of thanks to them, naming one way you have seen their faith or love grow, the way Paul does in verse 3.
1.prayer: Thank God for the people whose faith has held you up. Ask for steadiness for anyone in the group who is under pressure, and for trust that God sees what is unfair and will make it right.
1.tip: Verses 6 to 9 about vengeance and destruction can make people uneasy, and some may stay silent. Say up front that Christians read verse 9 differently, and that honest unease is welcome. Then bring the group back to the heart of the chapter: Paul writes to comfort people who are suffering, not to threaten them.

2.open: Have you ever heard a rumor that turned out to be completely wrong? What happened when the truth came out?
questions: Paul asks the Thessalonians "not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed" by claims that the Day of the Lord had already come (v. 2). What kinds of news or predictions tend to rattle you or the people around you?

The false claims came by "spirit or message or letter" (v. 2). Where do confident claims about God, the future or the end of the world reach us today, and how do you decide how much weight to give them?

Paul says certain things must happen first, including "the rebellion" and the revealing of "the man of lawlessness" (v. 3). What was Paul trying to do for these worried believers by telling them this?

Verse 5 asks, "Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you?" Paul's first readers knew what was restraining this figure, but we do not (v. 6). How do you feel about a passage that leaves us with unanswered questions?

Christians read the man of lawlessness in different ways: a single person still to come, a figure from Paul's own time, or a pattern of evil that keeps showing up. What stands out to you in verses 3 to 12 no matter which view you lean toward?

Verses 10 to 12 speak of people who "refused the love of the truth" and of God sending "a powerful delusion." Many readers take this to mean God confirms a choice people have already made. What do you make of that? If this passage stirs up doubt or fear for you, you can say so honestly.
Paul turns in verse 13 to say "God chose you from the beginning to be saved," and in verse 15 he says "stand firm." What does standing firm look like in an ordinary week, not just in a crisis?

In verses 16 and 17 Paul prays that Jesus and the Father, who "by grace has loved us," would "encourage your hearts and strengthen you." When have you felt that kind of steadying, and what did it come through?
2.life: This week, when you come across a dramatic claim about the future, in the news, online or from a friend, pause before you share it or worry about it. Ask whether it fits what Scripture clearly says, then read verses 16 and 17 and pray them for yourself or someone you know.
2.prayer: Thank God that he has loved us by grace and given us "eternal comfort and good hope." Ask him to steady anyone in the group who feels anxious about the future, and to give you wisdom to tell what is true.
2.tip: Verses 3 to 12 can pull a group into a long debate about who the man of lawlessness is or what restrains him. Say plainly that Christians disagree and that Paul's first readers knew more than we do. Then bring the group back to Paul's actual point: do not be shaken, and stand firm in Christ.

3.open: Who is someone you knew growing up who always showed up to help, and what did they do?
questions: Paul asks the church to pray "that the word of the Lord may spread quickly" (v. 1). What would it look like to pray that for the people and places around you?

Verse 3 says, "the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one." Where do you most need strength or protection right now? You can answer as honestly as you like, including if it is hard to feel that this is true.

Paul says he worked "night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (v. 8), though he had the right to be supported (v. 9). Why might he give up something he was owed? What does that tell you about how he led?
Paul had already taught, "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (v. 10). Notice that he says "unwilling," not "unable." Why does that difference matter for how we apply this today?

Some were "accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies" (v. 11). When have you seen a person's free time turn into gossip or meddling in other people's lives? What helps a person settle into their own work?
Paul says, "do not grow weary in well-doing" (v. 13). Where do you feel tired of helping or giving? What would help you keep going without resentment?

In verses 14 and 15 the church is to keep its distance from the person who ignores the instructions, "so that he may be ashamed," yet not "regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother." What would it look like to do both at once?
Paul ends by praying, "may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way" (v. 16). Where does your group, family or church most need peace right now?
3.life: Look for one practical way to help someone this week who is truly in need, such as a meal, a ride or an hour of your time. Also pay attention to your own habits: is there work you have been putting off or something you could take on quietly and faithfully?
3.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful and guards his people. Ask for a willingness to work, a generous heart that does not grow weary, and peace in your relationships.
3.tip: Verses 10 and 14 can be misused to judge people who are poor, sick, unemployed or caring for others at home. Point out that Paul is speaking to those who are unwilling, not unable, and that verse 15 keeps them in the family. Christians also read the cause of the idleness differently: some think members expected Jesus to return very soon, others think they were leaning on wealthier patrons. You can say so briefly and then keep the group on what the passage asks of all of us.
